summary: One of the four Panhellenic games sites, with a stadium whose vaulted entrance tunnel still bears athletes' graffiti.
significance: Preserves the physical mechanics of a Greek athletic festival better than any other site, including a starting gate.
body:
The Nemean Games were held every two years from 573 BC, third in prestige after Olympia and Delphi. In myth the sanctuary commemorated the infant Opheltes, killed by a snake, and Heracles killed the Nemean lion here.

The stadium has a vaulted entrance tunnel of c. 320 BC — an early true arch in Greek building — on whose walls athletes scratched their names, some 2,300 years ago. The starting line preserves sockets for the *hysplex*, a spring-loaded barrier that dropped simultaneously to give a fair start.

The Games were revived in 1996 as a public event in which anyone may run barefoot in a tunic on the ancient track.

name: Marathon

claims.text: Athenian and Plataean hoplites defeated a Persian force at Marathon in 490 BC.
The Soros mound covers the cremated Athenian dead of the battle.
Herodotus describes Pheidippides running to Sparta, not to Athens.
The story of a runner dying after announcing victory at Athens is a later tradition.

summary: The plain where Athenian hoplites defeated a Persian landing force in 490 BC, and the burial mound of the 192 Athenian dead.
significance: Proved Persian infantry could be beaten, and gave Athens a founding victory it celebrated for centuries.
body:
The *Soros*, a 9 m mound on the plain, covers the cremated Athenian dead. Excavation confirmed ash, burnt bone and vases of the right date — an unusual honour, since Athenians were normally buried in the state cemetery.

The Athenians ran the last stretch into the Persian archers to cross the killing zone quickly, then held the wings while the deliberately thinned centre gave ground, enveloping the Persians. Herodotus gives 6,400 Persian dead to 192 Athenian.

The modern marathon commemorates a run from here to Athens announcing the victory. Herodotus tells no such story — his runner, Pheidippides, ran to Sparta for help, about 240 km, which is far more remarkable and is now itself a race, the Spartathlon.

name: Thermopylae

claims.text: A Greek force under Leonidas held the pass at Thermopylae for three days in 480 BC.
Persian arrowheads were excavated on Kolonos hill, confirming the final stand location.
The ancient coastline has shifted several kilometres due to river sedimentation.

summary: The narrow coastal pass where Leonidas and his rearguard held Xerxes' army for three days in 480 BC.
significance: The archetypal last stand, and a rare case where archaeology has confirmed the location and the fighting.
body:
The pass was named for its hot sulphur springs, which still flow. In 480 BC it was a defile only a few metres wide between cliffs and sea; sediment from the Spercheios river has since pushed the coastline several kilometres out, so the battlefield is now an inland plain — one reason the site was long misidentified.

Spyridon Marinatos excavated Kolonos hill in the 1930s and found large numbers of Persian bronze arrowheads, confirming both the location and Herodotus' account that the last survivors were overwhelmed by missiles on the hill.

A later inscription records Simonides' couplet asking the passer-by to tell the Spartans that here they lie, obedient to their commands.

name: Chaeronea

claims.text: Philip II defeated an Athenian-Theban coalition at Chaeronea in 338 BC.
A mass grave of 254 men lies beneath the Lion of Chaeronea.
The burial is that of the Theban Sacred Band.
Alexander personally led the decisive cavalry charge.

summary: Where Philip II defeated the Greek alliance in 338 BC — and where a stone lion marks the grave of the Theban Sacred Band.
significance: The battle that ended the independence of the Greek city-states.
body:
Philip commanded the Macedonian right; the eighteen-year-old Alexander led the cavalry on the left. Philip drew the Athenians forward with a feigned withdrawal, opening a gap in the allied line into which Alexander charged.

The Sacred Band of Thebes — 150 pairs of male lovers, unbeaten for a generation — refused to retreat and was destroyed. Plutarch reports Philip weeping at the sight of their bodies.

In 1880 a colossal stone lion was reassembled on the site; excavation beneath it found 254 skeletons laid in seven rows. The identification with the Sacred Band is not certain but is very widely accepted.

name: Pydna

claims.text: A Roman army under Aemilius Paullus destroyed the Macedonian phalanx at Pydna in 168 BC.
The Macedonian kingdom was abolished after the battle.
Loss of phalanx cohesion on uneven ground was decisive.

summary: Where the Roman legion destroyed the Macedonian phalanx in 168 BC, ending the kingdom of Alexander's successors.
significance: The decisive demonstration that the legion had superseded the phalanx as the dominant infantry system.
body:
Perseus' phalanx initially drove the Romans back. But as it advanced over uneven ground the line lost cohesion and gaps opened. Aemilius Paullus ordered his maniples into those gaps, where legionaries with short swords got inside the reach of the pikes. Once past the pike points, a phalangite with both hands on a six-metre sarissa was defenceless.

Polybius, present in Rome and writing from participants' accounts, drew the lesson explicitly: the phalanx requires level unbroken ground and cannot adapt when it does not get it.

The kingdom of Macedon was abolished and divided into four republics; 150,000 people from Epirus were enslaved in the aftermath.

name: Actium

claims.text: Octavian's fleet defeated Antony and Cleopatra at Actium on 2 September 31 BC.
Cleopatra's squadron withdrew during the battle and Antony followed.
The victory monument at Nicopolis displayed captured ship rams in sockets that still survive.
The withdrawal was a pre-planned escape rather than a betrayal.

summary: The naval battle of 31 BC where Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra, ending both the Roman Republic and the Hellenistic age.
significance: The last battle of the Hellenistic world; within a year Egypt was a Roman province and Octavian was on his way to becoming Augustus.
body:
Antony and Cleopatra were blockaded in the Ambracian Gulf, their crews weakened by malaria and desertion. Antony tried to break out. Mid-battle Cleopatra's squadron of sixty ships raised sail and ran for Egypt; Antony followed, abandoning his fleet and army.

Whether this was a planned breakout that partly succeeded or a collapse is still argued — Octavian's version, which became the standard one, naturally emphasised betrayal and Antony's subjection to a foreign queen.

Octavian founded Nicopolis, "Victory City", nearby and built a monument displaying the rams of captured ships; the sockets survive, and their size confirms the ships were very large.

name: Pella

claims.text: Pella was the capital of Macedon from around 400 BC.
Its pebble mosaics of c. 300 BC are among the finest known.
Alexander the Great was born at Pella.
Euripides spent his final years at the Macedonian court.

summary: Capital of Macedon, birthplace of Alexander, and site of the finest pebble mosaics in the Greek world.
significance: The centre from which Macedon governed Greece and launched the conquest of Asia.
body:
Archelaus moved the Macedonian capital here around 400 BC and invited Greek artists — Zeuxis painted the palace, Euripides spent his last years and died here.

The pebble mosaics of c. 300 BC are made from natural coloured river stones set in cement, with lead strips for outlines: a stag hunt signed by Gnosis, a lion hunt, Dionysus riding a panther. The modelling of muscle and drapery in nothing but graded pebbles is remarkable.

Pella was connected to the sea by a navigable channel, since silted up. Alexander and probably Philip were born here; Philip was buried at the older royal centre of Aegae (Vergina).

name: Vergina

claims.text: An unlooted royal Macedonian tomb was excavated at Vergina in 1977.
Tomb II contained a gold larnax with cremated remains and a gold oak wreath.
The tomb dates to the second half of the 4th century BC.
Tomb II is the burial of Philip II.
Tomb II is the burial of Philip III Arrhidaeus.
The Great Tumulus covering the tombs is thought to have been raised deliberately, likely under Antigonus Gonatas, to protect them after a Celtic raid on Macedon in 279 BC.
A separate, smaller tomb at the site, Tomb I, had been looted in antiquity but retains a painted fresco of the abduction of Persephone.

summary: The old royal capital of Macedon, where an unlooted royal tomb was found in 1977 under a great mound.
significance: The richest unplundered royal burial ever excavated in Greece, and the strongest candidate for the tomb of Philip II.
body:
Manolis Andronikos excavated the Great Tumulus in 1977, a mound so large it had been assumed to be entirely natural, and found beneath it a barrel-vaulted tomb with an intact façade painted with a vivid hunting frieze, its marble doors still closed and its contents undisturbed by looters — an exceptional survival in a region where royal tombs were otherwise stripped bare within a generation or two of burial. The scale and placement of the tumulus itself, raised over at least two earlier tombs including one already looted in antiquity, is now generally thought to have been a deliberate act of protection, probably ordered by Antigonus Gonatas after a Celtic raid devastated Macedon in 279 BC, burying the royal tombs under enough earth to hide and secure them from further disturbance.

Inside the unlooted tomb: a marble sarcophagus containing a solid gold *larnax* embossed with the sixteen-rayed Macedonian star, holding cremated bones wrapped in a purple cloth with a separate gold oak wreath laid on top. Also present were an iron and gold cuirass, a ceremonial shield, an extensive set of silver dining vessels, and five small ivory portrait heads, one of which is strikingly similar to known images of Philip II. A neighbouring, smaller tomb at the same site, conventionally labelled Tomb I, had already been looted in antiquity but still preserves on its walls a rare and beautifully painted fresco of the abduction of Persephone by Hades, one of the finest surviving examples of large-scale Greek painting from any period.

The identification of the main tomb's occupant is genuinely contested. Supporters of a Philip II attribution point to the ivory head's resemblance, to leg greaves of conspicuously unequal length matching an old, documented battle wound of Philip's, and to the burial's apparent date. Opponents argue, based on the vault's architectural type and associated pottery, that the burial actually belongs a generation later, to Philip III Arrhidaeus, murdered in the succession wars after Alexander's death. Separate scientific studies of the skeletal remains in 2015 and again in 2024 have produced flatly conflicting conclusions about age, sex and old injuries. What can be said with confidence is only that the tomb is unmistakably royal, unmistakably Macedonian, and dates to the mid-to-late fourth century BC; beyond that, the identity of its occupant remains a genuinely open scholarly question rather than a settled fact.

name: Alexandria

claims.text: Alexandria was founded by Alexander in 331 BC and became the Ptolemaic capital.
The Museum salaried resident scholars who produced major scientific work.
The Pharos lighthouse stood over 100 m tall; blocks have been recovered underwater.
The Library declined gradually rather than being destroyed in one fire.
The Library held hundreds of thousands of scrolls.
The location of Alexander's tomb is known.
Ships docking at Alexandria were reportedly required to hand over any scrolls aboard for copying by the Library, keeping only the copy while the original was retained.
Alexandria's population included large, distinct Greek, Egyptian and Jewish communities, and produced the Septuagint, the Hebrew Bible's Greek translation.

summary: Alexander's greatest foundation: capital of Ptolemaic Egypt, home of the Library, the Museum and the Pharos lighthouse.
significance: The intellectual capital of the ancient Mediterranean for three centuries, where most Greek science was done.
body:
Alexander chose the site himself in 331 BC, reportedly picking a strip of land between the sea and Lake Mareotis specifically for its two harbours and reliable fresh water, then left before construction had properly begun; it was Ptolemy I and his son who actually built the city and made it Egypt's capital in place of the ancient inland city of Memphis. Its grid plan, laid out by the architect Dinocrates, was deliberately oriented to catch the prevailing sea breeze off the Mediterranean, a detail of urban planning meant to make the city liveable in Egyptian heat in a way few older Mediterranean cities had ever been designed for.

The Museum — literally a "shrine of the Muses," the origin of the modern word museum despite functioning much more like a state-funded research institute — salaried resident scholars, housed and fed them at communal expense, and left them largely free to pursue their own research rather than teach or perform administrative duties. Euclid systematised geometry there, Eratosthenes measured the Earth's circumference, Aristarchus proposed a heliocentric model centuries before Copernicus, Herophilus pioneered human dissection, and Apollonius of Perga wrote the definitive ancient treatment of conic sections — a concentration of theoretical achievement no other single institution in the ancient world came close to matching. Its attached Library pursued acquisition as aggressively as the Museum pursued research: ships docking in Alexandria's harbour were reportedly required to surrender any scrolls on board to be copied, with the ship's owner receiving only the copy back while the original stayed in the Library's own collection, and Ptolemaic agents are said to have gone still further, borrowing official Athenian master copies of the great tragedians against an enormous security deposit and then simply forfeiting the deposit and keeping the originals. Modern estimates of the Library's total holdings range anywhere from 40,000 to as many as 700,000 scrolls, and every figure in that range is ultimately an informed guess rather than a documented count.

The city's population was never simply Greek. Distinct and substantial Greek, native Egyptian and Jewish communities lived alongside each other, each with its own quarter, and the city's Jewish community was large and Greek-speaking enough that it produced the Septuagint, a Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible undertaken specifically because most Alexandrian Jews could no longer read Hebrew fluently — one of Alexandria's most consequential intellectual products, and one owing nothing to the Museum's Greek scholars at all.

The Pharos lighthouse, over 100 metres tall and counted among the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, guided ships into the harbour for some seventeen centuries until a sequence of earthquakes finally brought it down in the fourteenth century AD; underwater archaeologists have been recovering its fallen masonry, along with sphinxes and obelisks, from the harbour floor since systematic diving surveys began there in 1994. The Library's own end was far less dramatic than its popular reputation suggests: rather than vanishing in a single catastrophic fire, as later legend generally has it, it declined gradually across several centuries through a harbour fire during Julius Caesar's occupation in 48 BC that damaged some holdings, the slow withdrawal of Ptolemaic and then Roman royal patronage, and the eventual departure or expulsion of the scholars who had once been paid to stay — attrition rather than a single catastrophe, though a far less satisfying story than the one that survives in popular memory.

name: Memphis

claims.text: Memphis remained a major Egyptian city for more than three millennia.
It was the principal cult centre of the god Ptah.
Alexander participated in royal and religious ceremonies at Memphis.
The Memphis Decree of 196 BC survives in multiple copies, including the Rosetta Stone.

summary: The ancient capital near the head of the Nile Delta and the principal cult centre of Ptah.
significance: A political and religious centre for more than three millennia, including under Persian, Macedonian and Ptolemaic rule.
body:
Memphis stood near the point where the Nile divides into its Delta branches, a strategic position between Upper Egypt, the Delta and the routes west towards the Fayyum. Tradition credited its foundation to Menes, the legendary unifier of Egypt; archaeology instead reveals a settlement and royal landscape that developed across the earliest dynasties. The nearby pyramid fields at Saqqara, Abusir and Giza belonged to this Memphite political and ceremonial world.

It was the principal cult centre of Ptah, patron of craftspeople, whose great temple gave the city one of its Egyptian names, Hut-ka-Ptah. Greek speakers ultimately used a related form for the country itself: *Aigyptos*. Even when royal residences moved elsewhere, Memphis retained workshops, temples, garrisons and a priesthood able to confer Egyptian legitimacy.

Assyrians, Persians and Macedonians all treated possession of Memphis as politically meaningful. Alexander was recognised there after entering Egypt in 332 BC. The Ptolemies ruled from Alexandria but continued to patronise Ptah’s temple; the Memphis Decree of 196 BC, preserved most famously on the Rosetta Stone, records priests honouring Ptolemy V in the traditional idiom of Egyptian kingship.

name: Thebes (Waset)

claims.text: Waset was a principal royal centre during the Middle and New Kingdoms.
Karnak remained one of Egypt’s most important temple complexes throughout this atlas’s period.
Assyrian forces sacked Thebes in 663 BC.

summary: The great Upper Egyptian city of Karnak and Luxor, capital of the New Kingdom at its height.
significance: Egypt’s dominant religious centre and the monumental setting of New Kingdom power encountered by the wider Bronze Age world.
body:
The Egyptian city called Waset—later Thebes to Greek speakers—occupied both banks of the Nile around modern Luxor. The living city and the great temples stood mainly on the east bank; royal mortuary temples and the cemeteries now called the Valleys of the Kings and Queens spread across the western desert edge.

Local rulers reunified Egypt at the beginning of the Middle Kingdom, giving Thebes its first period of national power. It became the ceremonial heart of the New Kingdom after another Theban dynasty expelled the Hyksos. Karnak’s temple of Amun grew through centuries of additions into a monumental record of royal competition, while Luxor Temple was central to the Opet festival that renewed divine and royal authority.

Political capitals later moved north, but Thebes remained wealthy through its temples, estates and priesthood. Akhenaten challenged that establishment; Tutankhamun restored it. Assyrian forces sacked the city in 663 BC, yet its sanctuaries continued to attract patronage under later Egyptian, Persian, Macedonian and Ptolemaic rulers. The visible landscape is therefore not one moment but the accumulation of more than a millennium of building, erasure and reuse.

name: Canopus

claims.text: Canopus was an important religious and maritime centre in the western Nile Delta.
Its cult landscape combined Egyptian and Greek religious forms in the Ptolemaic period.
The identification of Canopus in Abu Qir Bay is supported by inscriptions and underwater archaeology.

summary: A western Delta port and pilgrimage centre later absorbed into Alexandria’s maritime hinterland.
significance: A major meeting place for Egyptian and Greek religious traditions near the Canopic mouth of the Nile.
body:
Canopus lay east of Alexandria near the westernmost mouth of the Nile and was linked by canals to neighbouring Thonis-Heracleion. Its Egyptian sacred landscape centred on Osiris, while Greek tradition named the place for Canopus, the helmsman of Menelaus who was supposedly buried there after dying from a snakebite. The story is an aetiology, not a recoverable foundation history.

Under the Ptolemies the city became part of Alexandria’s maritime and religious hinterland. The annual Mysteries of Osiris involved processions and ritual vessels moving between sanctuaries around the bay. Greek and Egyptian inscriptions, images and architectural forms occur together, showing interaction without requiring that the two religious traditions simply merged into one.

Earthquakes, liquefaction, subsidence and rising water gradually submerged much of the settlement. Underwater survey in Abu Qir Bay has recovered colossal statuary, temple blocks, inscriptions, coins and ritual equipment. These finds restore Canopus as a substantial cult and harbour centre rather than the pleasure resort emphasised by some later Greek and Roman writers.

name: Thonis-Heracleion

claims.text: Thonis and Heracleion were Egyptian and Greek names for the same port city.
The city controlled a major maritime entrance into Egypt before Alexandria.
Underwater excavations have documented dozens of ancient vessels around the submerged city.

summary: The port at the Canopic Nile mouth that controlled maritime entry into Egypt before Alexandria.
significance: A principal customs and exchange point between Egypt and the Mediterranean before Alexandria displaced it.
body:
Egyptian Thonis and Greek Heracleion were two names for the same port city at the mouth of the Canopic branch. A bilingual decree and other inscriptions settled what had once been treated as a question of two neighbouring settlements. Before Alexandria existed, ships arriving from the Greek world entered here, declared their cargoes and passed through a controlled gateway to the Nile network.

The city combined commercial infrastructure with major sanctuaries, especially a temple of Amun-Gereb connected to royal legitimacy. Finds of imported ceramics, weights, coins and more than sixty ancient shipwrecks reveal traffic on a scale that literary descriptions alone could not establish. Naukratis lay farther inland and operated within the same exchange system rather than serving as a simple rival port.

Alexandria redirected much of this traffic after 331 BC, but Thonis-Heracleion did not immediately disappear. It remained active into the Ptolemaic and Roman periods before unstable delta sediments, earthquakes and subsidence placed large areas beneath Abu Qir Bay. Underwater excavation has recovered the urban plan, monumental sculpture and ritual deposits in their archaeological context.

name: Pergamon

claims.text: Pergamon was the Attalid capital, built in terraces up a steep acropolis.
The Great Altar frieze depicts the battle of gods and giants in high relief.
Attalus III bequeathed the kingdom to Rome in 133 BC.
Parchment takes its name from Pergamon.
Parchment was invented at Pergamon because of a papyrus embargo.

summary: Attalid capital on a steep acropolis, with the steepest theatre in the ancient world, a great altar, and a library that rivalled Alexandria's.
significance: The showpiece of Hellenistic urban design and of the dramatic "Pergamene baroque" sculptural style.
body:
The Attalids built Pergamon up a 300 m acropolis in terraces. Its theatre is cut into the slope at an extraordinary angle, seating 10,000 in 80 rows.

The Great Altar of c. 160 BC carries a 113 m frieze of gods fighting giants, carved in violent high relief with figures breaking out of the architecture — a coded celebration of Attalid victories over the Galatians. The German excavation removed it to Berlin, where it remains, and Turkey continues to seek its return.

When the Ptolemies restricted papyrus exports to hamper the rival library, Pergamon developed treated animal skin as a writing surface. The Latin *pergamena* — parchment — records the origin. The last Attalid king bequeathed the kingdom to Rome in 133 BC.

name: Rhodes

claims.text: Rhodes withstood the siege of Demetrius Poliorcetes in 305–304 BC.
The Colossus of Rhodes stood roughly 33 m tall and fell in an earthquake c. 226 BC.
Rhodian maritime law influenced Roman and later admiralty law.
The Colossus straddled the harbour entrance.
The Antikythera mechanism was made in a Rhodian workshop.

summary: A naval and commercial power whose Colossus was one of the Seven Wonders, and whose maritime law Rome adopted.
significance: Survived one of antiquity's greatest sieges and set the legal standards for Mediterranean shipping.
body:
In 305–304 BC Demetrius Poliorcetes besieged Rhodes with siege towers including the *Helepolis*, a nine-storey armoured tower 40 m high moved by 3,400 men. The Rhodians held. Demetrius left his equipment behind, and they sold it to fund the Colossus — a 33 m bronze statue of Helios that stood about 54 years before an earthquake toppled it in 226 BC. It did not straddle the harbour; that image is medieval invention.

Rhodian sea law on jettison and shared loss was adopted into Roman law and survives in modern admiralty practice as general average. The Antikythera mechanism is often attributed to a Rhodian workshop, where Hipparchus and later Posidonius worked.

name: Salamis

claims.text: Salamis was traditionally founded by Teucer after the Trojan War.
Salamis was the leading city-kingdom of Cyprus by the Classical period.
Its king Nicocreon allied with Ptolemy I during the Wars of the Diadochi.

summary: The wealthiest of Cyprus's ancient city-kingdoms, and the harbour where a 306 BC naval battle helped launch the Hellenistic age of independent kings.
significance: Traditional capital of Cypriot Salamis; its 306 BC battle reshaped the political vocabulary of the entire Hellenistic world.
body:
Greek tradition held that Salamis was founded by Teucer, the archer of the Trojan War exiled from the island of Salamis in the Saronic Gulf and unable to go home to a father who blamed him for his brother Ajax's death — one of the stock post-war founding stories, but a genuinely old one.

By the Classical period it was the largest and richest of Cyprus's city-kingdoms, its kings striking their own coinage and playing the larger Mediterranean powers against each other. Nicocreon, its last king, backed Ptolemy I in the wars after Alexander's death.

That choice proved costly. In 306 BC Demetrius Poliorcetes attacked the island, defeated a Ptolemaic fleet in the harbour, and took the city — the battle that pushed Antigonus I to claim the title of king outright.

name: Palaepaphos

claims.text: Palaepaphos was a major Cypriot city-kingdom and sanctuary centre.
The sanctuary of Aphrodite has Late Bronze Age origins.
Kings of Paphos held a priestly role connected with the sanctuary.
A returning Trojan War hero founded Palaepaphos.

summary: Old Paphos, a Cypriot city-kingdom and the long-lived sanctuary centre of Aphrodite.
significance: One of the principal Cypriot kingdoms and the cult centre most closely associated with Aphrodite.
body:
Palaepaphos occupied the coastal plain around modern Kouklia, close to routes leading inland towards the copper-bearing Troodos foothills. It became the seat of one of Cyprus’s city-kingdoms and the island’s most renowned sanctuary of the goddess whom Greek visitors identified as Aphrodite. Worship at the sanctuary reaches back into the Late Bronze Age, although its rites and divine names changed across that long history.

The cult image was not the familiar nude goddess of later art but an aniconic stone. Kings of Paphos also served as priests, binding political authority to the sanctuary. Inscriptions and coinage show a Greek-speaking kingdom using the Cypriot syllabary, while its material culture remained connected to both the Aegean and the Levant.

Ancient foundation stories credited Agapenor, returning from Troy, with founding the city. They reveal how later communities explained their identity; they do not document a named Bronze Age founder. Near the end of the fourth century BC King Nicocles established Nea Paphos by a better harbour. Administration moved, but the old sanctuary remained powerful under the Ptolemies and Romans, and images of its sacred stone appeared on Roman Cypriot coinage.

name: Nea Paphos

claims.text: Nea Paphos was founded near the end of the 4th century BC.
It became the administrative capital of Ptolemaic Cyprus.
The so-called Tombs of the Kings were elite burials rather than a cemetery of ruling kings.

summary: The harbour city that replaced Palaepaphos as western Cyprus’s political centre and became the Ptolemaic capital of the island.
significance: The principal administrative and maritime centre of Hellenistic Cyprus.
body:
Nicocles, the last king of Palaepaphos, established a new planned city beside a natural harbour near the end of the fourth century BC. The move did not abolish Old Paphos or its sanctuary: it created a maritime administrative centre while the older sacred centre continued inland. A gridded street plan, fortifications and harbour works connected the foundation to the wider urban transformation of the early Hellenistic Mediterranean.

After the Ptolemies eliminated the Cypriot kingships, Nea Paphos became the headquarters of the governor or *strategos* who administered the whole island from Egypt. Its position facing Alexandria made it a practical naval and fiscal capital. Coinage, inscriptions and imported goods show that it participated in Ptolemaic institutions while retaining Cypriot religious traditions.

The monumental record spans many centuries. The rock-cut “Tombs of the Kings” belonged to high officials rather than literal kings; the theatre began in the Hellenistic period and was repeatedly altered; elaborate mosaic houses belong mainly to Roman prosperity. Paphos retained its leading status after Rome annexed Cyprus, so the surviving city should not be mistaken for a purely Ptolemaic snapshot.

name: Kition

claims.text: Kition was occupied as a major centre from the Late Bronze Age.
It was a principal Phoenician-speaking kingdom of Iron Age Cyprus.
The kings of Kition acquired Idalion during the 5th century BC.

summary: A major south-coast harbour whose Bronze Age settlement became a Phoenician-led Cypriot city-kingdom.
significance: One of Cyprus’s principal ports and the island’s strongest centre of Phoenician language and cult.
body:
Kition developed around sheltered harbours at modern Larnaca. Late Bronze Age occupation included monumental buildings, industrial areas and evidence for processing copper brought from the island’s interior. Imported pottery and other finds place the settlement within maritime networks joining Cyprus to the Levant, Egypt and the Aegean before any historically documented kingdom existed.

Phoenician language and institutions became especially prominent during the early first millennium BC. Inscriptions name kings and deities such as Astarte and Reshef-Mikal, while Greek and Cypriot traditions remained present around them. It is therefore more accurate to describe Kition as a Phoenician-led Cypriot kingdom than as a foreign colony that replaced an empty landscape.

Its rulers expanded inland and absorbed Idalion in the fifth century BC, gaining access to copper routes and agricultural territory. A fourth-century Phoenician inscription records a king of “Kition and Idalion” commemorating victory. The kingdom participated in the shifting Assyrian, Egyptian and Persian systems that claimed authority over Cyprus, then lost its monarchy when Ptolemaic administration unified the island.

name: Kourion

claims.text: Kourion was one of the principal city-kingdoms of ancient Cyprus.
Its inhabitants linked their origins with settlers from Argos.
The sanctuary of Apollo Hylates served as a major regional cult centre.

summary: A hilltop city-kingdom commanding the fertile Kouris valley on Cyprus’s southern coast.
significance: One of the island’s principal kingdoms, with a commanding acropolis and long-lived sanctuary landscape.
body:
Kourion stood on a high coastal ridge overlooking the Kouris valley, with farmland below and access to the south-coast sea lanes. Settlement and rich burial evidence at nearby Bamboula connect the district with the transformations of the twelfth century BC. Later Greek tradition claimed settlers from Argos, but archaeology shows cultural change and continuing local development rather than a single recoverable migration event.

By the Iron Age Kourion was one of Cyprus’s city-kingdoms. Its rulers issued coinage and negotiated the same layers of Assyrian, Egyptian and Persian supremacy as their neighbours. The kingdom’s territory linked the coast to inland resources, while the extra-urban sanctuary of Apollo Hylates became a durable regional cult centre.

Most monuments visible on the acropolis—the theatre in its surviving form, bath buildings, mosaics and episcopal complex—are Hellenistic, Roman or later. They overlie the political centre of the earlier kingdom rather than illustrating it directly. Keeping those phases separate matters: an impressive Roman cityscape cannot by itself reconstruct the institutions or boundaries of Archaic Kourion.

name: Amathous

claims.text: Amathous was a major city-kingdom of Iron Age Cyprus.
A prominent sanctuary of Aphrodite-Astarte stood on its acropolis.
Eteocypriot inscriptions from Amathous preserve a non-Greek language that remains only partly understood.

summary: A major south-coast kingdom with distinctive local traditions and a prominent cult of Aphrodite-Astarte.
significance: A durable Cypriot kingdom whose material culture preserves especially strong local and Levantine connections.
body:
Amathous occupied a coastal acropolis east of modern Limassol, with a lower town and harbour below. It emerged as one of the island’s principal Iron Age kingdoms but resisted the easy foundation labels attached to other Cypriot cities. Later sources treated its inhabitants as indigenous, and inscriptions preserve the undeciphered Eteocypriot language alongside Greek.

The acropolis sanctuary housed a goddess whom Greek speakers identified with Aphrodite and whose imagery also drew on Levantine traditions. Monumental stone vessels, tombs and sculpture display local choices rather than a passive mixture of supposedly “Greek” and “Phoenician” elements. The city’s political identity likewise remained distinct while its kings operated within Assyrian, Egyptian and Persian spheres of supremacy.

Amathous survived the abolition of the kingdoms under Ptolemy I as a prosperous town and cult centre. Its harbour connected the south coast to regional trade, and under Rome it remained one of Cyprus’s principal urban centres alongside Paphos and Salamis. The standing agora and baths are largely later than the independent kingdom and must be read as another phase in the same long-lived settlement.

name: Idalion

claims.text: Idalion was an important inland city-kingdom of Cyprus.
Its inscriptions attest both Cypriot Greek and Phoenician.
The Idalion Tablet records a public agreement rewarding physicians who treated battle casualties.

summary: An inland Cypriot kingdom controlling copper-working country south of the Mesaoria plain.
significance: Its bilingual and Cypriot-syllabic inscriptions are central evidence for the island’s languages and political institutions.
body:
Idalion was an inland city-kingdom centred on two acropoleis near modern Dali. Its location commanded routes between the Mesaoria plain, the south coast and copper-producing districts in the Troodos foothills. Sanctuaries, fortifications, workshops and cemeteries reveal an urban community whose importance did not depend on possessing a seaport.

The bronze Idalion Tablet records a contract between the king and the city concerning doctors who treated the wounded during a siege. Written in Greek using the Cypriot syllabary, it is unusually direct evidence for civic institutions, landholding and public obligation. Phoenician inscriptions from the area document another language and cult tradition within the same political landscape.

Kition absorbed the kingdom during the fifth century BC. Later inscriptions style its ruler “king of Kition and Idalion,” making the loss of independence visible in contemporary evidence rather than only in later narrative. Settlement and sanctuary activity continued after annexation and under the Ptolemies, so political extinction did not mean that the place or its population vanished.

name: Syracuse

claims.text: Syracuse was founded from Corinth in 734 BC.
The Athenian expedition of 415–413 BC was destroyed at Syracuse.
Surviving Athenians were imprisoned in the stone quarries.
Archimedes designed defensive machines used in the siege of 213–212 BC.
The torsion catapult was developed at Syracuse under Dionysius I.
Cicero described Syracuse as the greatest and most beautiful of all Greek cities.
Syracuse fell to Rome after a night assault exploited a lapse in the city's defences during a festival.

summary: The greatest Greek city of the west, which destroyed an Athenian invasion force and was later defended by Archimedes.
significance: Demonstrated that the Greek world's centre of gravity was not confined to the Aegean.
body:
Founded from Corinth in 734 BC, Syracuse grew over the following centuries into a city the Roman orator Cicero, writing generations after its independence had ended, still called the greatest and most beautiful of all Greek cities, praising above all its natural double harbour and the freshwater spring of Arethusa rising, according to myth, straight out of the sea on the small island at its centre.

In 415–413 BC Athens sent an enormous naval and land expedition to conquer it, hoping to add Sicily's wealth and grain to its own empire. The siege failed disastrously: the Athenian fleet was trapped inside the Great Harbour and destroyed there, and the surviving soldiers, denied even the mercy of a quick death, were driven into the city's stone quarries, the *latomie*, and left there for weeks with minimal food or water until most died — the quarries themselves are still visible today, cut deep into the rock above the modern city. Thucydides calls the entire campaign the greatest single action of the whole war and the most calamitous for the losing side of any event he records.

Under the later tyrant Dionysius I, Syracuse built the largest fortifications anywhere in the Greek world at Euryalus, guarding the high ground above the city, and is credited by ancient sources with developing an early form of catapult for use in siege warfare. Nearly two centuries later, Archimedes designed remarkably effective defensive devices against a besieging Roman fleet and army in 213–212 BC, reportedly including grappling devices capable of lifting enemy ships bodily out of the water; the city held out for two full years regardless and finally fell only to a night assault that exploited a lapse in the garrison's vigilance during a religious festival. Archimedes himself, according to tradition, was killed by a Roman soldier during the ensuing sack while absorbed in a geometric diagram drawn in the sand, reportedly protesting only that the man should not disturb his circles.

name: Paestum

claims.text: Paestum preserves three Doric temples standing to entablature level.
The Tomb of the Diver is the only known Greek painted figural tomb of c. 470 BC.
The city was founded by Greeks from Sybaris around 600 BC.
The diving figure represents the soul's passage to the afterlife.

summary: A Greek colony in southern Italy with three of the best-preserved Doric temples anywhere, and a unique painted tomb.
significance: Its temples survive more completely than any in Greece, and its Tomb of the Diver is the only surviving Greek painted figural tomb of its era.
body:
Founded by Greeks from Sybaris around 600 BC as Poseidonia, the city has three Doric temples standing to their entablatures, spanning roughly 550–450 BC — a visible sequence of the order maturing from heavy archaic proportions to classical balance.

The Tomb of the Diver, found in 1968, has five painted slabs: a symposium on the walls and, on the lid, a young man diving into water. It is the only known Greek painted tomb with figural scenes from this period, and the dive is generally read as a metaphor for passing from life to death — though nothing in the tomb says so.

Malaria and the shifting coastline emptied the site in late antiquity, which is why the temples were never quarried.

name: Ai-Khanoum

claims.text: Ai-Khanoum was a Greek city in Bactria with a theatre, gymnasium and Greek inscriptions.
An inscription records Delphic maxims copied and brought there by Clearchus.
The city was destroyed around 145 BC.
The site has been severely damaged by looting since 1979.

summary: A fully Greek city on the Oxus in Afghanistan, with a gymnasium, theatre, and Delphic maxims inscribed 5,000 km from Delphi.
significance: The clearest proof that Hellenistic Greek civic culture was transplanted whole into Central Asia.
body:
Excavated by the French mission from 1964 until the Soviet invasion in 1979, Ai-Khanoum had a theatre for 6,000, a gymnasium, Corinthian-columned buildings and a palace on a Persian plan — Greek institutions in Achaemenid architectural dress.

In a *heroon* was a stone inscribed with maxims from Delphi, ending with a note that one Clearchus copied them at Delphi and set them up here. Someone carried the sayings of the Greek homeland across a continent so that a city on the Oxus could read them.

The library yielded impressions of a lost philosophical text left in the soil as papyrus decayed. The city was destroyed by nomadic invasion around 145 BC. The site was heavily looted during the Afghan wars and much is now unrecoverable.

name: Antioch

claims.text: Antioch was founded by Seleucus I in 300 BC as a Seleucid capital.
It became one of the largest cities of the ancient Mediterranean.
Much of the ancient city is inaccessible beneath modern settlement and river silt.

summary: Seleucid capital on the Orontes, one of the largest cities of the ancient world and a hub of Greek-Semitic exchange.
significance: The western capital of the Seleucid Empire and one of the great cities of the Mediterranean for a thousand years.
body:
Seleucus I founded Antioch in 300 BC, naming it for his father. Positioned where the Orontes valley meets routes to the Mediterranean and Mesopotamia, it grew to several hundred thousand people.

It was among the first cities anywhere with street lighting at night and a colonnaded main avenue several kilometres long. Its suburb Daphne, with springs and a sanctuary of Apollo, was famous for luxury.

Most of ancient Antioch lies under modern Antakya and deep river silt, so it is far less known archaeologically than its importance warrants. A large number of Roman-era floor mosaics have been recovered.

name: Cyrene

claims.text: Cyrene was founded from Thera around 631 BC.
Its economy depended heavily on the export of silphium.
Silphium became extinct by the 1st century AD.
Silphium could not be successfully cultivated outside its native range.
The heart symbol derives from the silphium seed pod.

summary: A Greek colony in North Africa that grew rich on silphium, a medicinal plant harvested to extinction.
significance: One of the most successful Greek colonies, and the site of the first recorded human-caused extinction of a commercial species.
body:
Founded from Thera around 631 BC after a drought, reportedly at the direction of the Delphic oracle. Cyrene became wealthy, producing the philosopher Aristippus and the mathematician Eratosthenes.

Its wealth rested on silphium, a plant used as seasoning, medicine and contraceptive, which grew only in a narrow coastal strip and resisted cultivation. Cyrenean coins depict it, and its seed pod — heart-shaped — is one proposed origin of the heart symbol. Overharvesting drove it to extinction by the first century AD; Pliny records that the last stalk was sent to the emperor Nero as a curiosity.

name: Massalia

claims.text: Massalia was founded by Phocaean Greeks around 600 BC.
Greek trade goods from Massalia reached deep into central Gaul.
Pytheas of Massalia sailed to Britain and northern waters c. 325 BC.
Pytheas correctly linked tides to the Moon.
Thule can be identified with a specific modern location.

summary: A Phocaean colony at the mouth of the Rhône that brought wine, the vine and the alphabet to Gaul.
significance: The westernmost major Greek city, and the base from which Pytheas sailed to Britain and the Arctic.
body:
Founded around 600 BC by Greeks from Phocaea in Ionia, Massalia controlled the Rhône trade route into central Europe. Greek wine amphorae from Massalia are found far up the river system, and the Vix krater — a 1.65 m bronze wine vessel found in a Celtic princess's grave in Burgundy — reflects this trade.

Around 325 BC the Massaliote Pytheas sailed out through Gibraltar, circumnavigated Britain, described tides correctly as linked to the Moon, and reported a land called Thule six days north where the sea became sluggish and the sun barely set. Ancient authors mostly disbelieved him. Modern readers, noting his accuracy on tides and latitude, generally do not.

name: Byzantion

claims.text: Byzantion was founded from Megara around 667 BC.
It controlled the Bosporus grain route from the Black Sea.
Athenian food security depended on Black Sea grain imports.

summary: A Megarian colony on the Bosporus controlling the grain route from the Black Sea to Greece.
significance: Its position made it strategically decisive in antiquity and imperial capital of the world for a millennium afterwards.
body:
Founded around 667 BC by settlers from Megara. Herodotus records the Persian general Megabazus calling the earlier colonists of Chalcedon, on the opposite shore, blind — because they had picked the inferior site when the best position in the world was visible across the water.

Whoever held Byzantion held the Bosporus, and therefore the grain shipments from the Black Sea on which Athens depended. Control of this route is a recurring strategic thread through Greek history, and cutting it is how Sparta finally won the Peloponnesian War.

Constantine refounded the city as his capital in AD 330.

name: Naukratis

claims.text: Naukratis was the designated port for Greek trade in Egypt from the 7th century BC.
Greeks from multiple cities shared a sanctuary there.
Archaic Greek kouros sculpture follows Egyptian proportional conventions.
Greek sculptors learned the Egyptian proportional grid directly at Naukratis.

summary: The single port where Egypt permitted Greek merchants to trade, and the main channel of Egyptian influence on Greek art.
significance: Where Greeks encountered monumental Egyptian stone sculpture — and began carving kouroi.
body:
Pharaoh Amasis concentrated all Greek trade with Egypt at Naukratis, where Greeks from a dozen cities shared a sanctuary called the Hellenion. It was a controlled interface rather than a colony: Egypt got the goods and taxes without Greeks spreading through the country.

The influence ran strongly the other way in art. The Archaic Greek *kouros* — nude male, left foot advanced, arms at sides, fists clenched — follows Egyptian conventions closely enough that transmission is not in doubt. Egyptian sculptors used a fixed proportional grid, and Diodorus reports that Greeks learned it here.

The site also produced faience, scarabs and a great deal of imported Greek pottery, making it one of the best-dated Archaic assemblages anywhere.

name: Al Mina

claims.text: Greek pottery, mainly Euboean, appears at Al Mina from around 800 BC.
The site indicates renewed Aegean–Levantine contact in the early Iron Age.
A resident Greek trading community lived at Al Mina.

summary: A trading settlement at the mouth of the Orontes where Greek pottery appears from the eighth century BC — the likely conduit of the alphabet.
significance: The clearest archaeological evidence for renewed Greek contact with the Near East just as the alphabet arrives in Greece.
body:
Leonard Woolley excavated Al Mina in 1936 and found Euboean Greek pottery in quantity from around 800 BC — precisely when Greeks adopt the Phoenician script.

Whether Greeks lived here or their pots simply arrived through Phoenician middlemen is disputed, and it matters: the first is a Greek trading community abroad, the second is Greeks receiving goods passively. The pottery includes drinking and mixing vessels, which suggests people using them rather than trade goods in transit.

Either way, the site marks the reopening of eastern contacts after the Bronze Age collapse, and the "orientalising" transformation of Greek art follows within a generation.

name: Poliochni

claims.text: Poliochni was a fortified Early Bronze Age town with streets, drainage and a public well.
A building with tiered stone benches has been identified there.
A gold hoard comparable to finds at Troy was recovered.
The tiered building functioned as an assembly hall.

summary: An Early Bronze Age town on Lemnos with a stone-built assembly hall, sometimes called the oldest town in Europe.
significance: Its tiered public hall is the earliest known purpose-built space for collective decision-making in Europe.
body:
Poliochni was fortified with stone walls, laid out with paved streets, drainage and a public well, and organised into blocks of adjoining houses — a genuine town, contemporary with the earliest phases of Troy across the water.

One building contains stone benches in tiers along the walls facing an open floor, seating perhaps fifty. It is normally interpreted as an assembly hall, which would make it the oldest known council chamber in Europe by two thousand years. The interpretation rests on the architecture alone; there are no inscriptions.

A hoard of gold jewellery closely resembling Schliemann's "Priam's Treasure" from Troy was found here, showing the two communities shared a metalworking tradition.

name: Chalandriani

claims.text: Chalandriani is a large Early Cycladic cemetery of stone cist graves.
"Frying pan" vessels engraved with multi-oared longships were found there.
The engravings depict long, many-oared vessels capable of open-sea travel.
The function of the frying pans is unknown.

summary: A large Early Cycladic cemetery and fortified settlement, source of the "frying pan" vessels engraved with longships.
significance: Its engraved ships are the earliest detailed depictions of Aegean seagoing vessels.
body:
Over 600 graves have been excavated at Chalandriani, small stone-lined cists containing marble figurines, obsidian blades and pottery.

The "frying pans" — flat circular clay objects with a forked handle, engraved with spirals, stars and longships — are the most distinctive Cycladic artefacts after the figurines. The ships are shown with dozens of oars, a high prow and a fish standard, and they establish that Early Bronze Age Cycladic vessels were long, many-oared and built for open water rather than coasting.

What the frying pans were for is unknown: mirrors filled with water, drums, salt pans and ritual objects have all been proposed. The nearby settlement at Kastri is fortified with bastions, indicating that this maritime world was competitive.

name: Persepolis

claims.text: Persepolis was built as an Achaemenid ceremonial capital from c. 518 BC.
Its staircase reliefs depict tribute delegations from subject peoples.
Administrative tablets record rations paid to workers including women.
The palace complex was destroyed by fire in 330 BC.
The burning was a deliberate act of policy rather than a drunken accident.

summary: The Achaemenid ceremonial capital, built by Darius I and burned by Alexander in 330 BC.
significance: The finest surviving Achaemenid architecture, and its destruction is the symbolic end of the Persian Empire.
body:
Persepolis stands on a terrace with monumental staircases whose reliefs show delegations from twenty-three subject peoples bringing tribute — Ethiopians with an okapi, Indians with gold, Armenians with a horse. It is an imperial statement of scale and order, and the figures are shown as dignified rather than subjugated.

Administrative tablets found in the fortifications record wages paid to workers, including women, in grain and wine, with extra rations for new mothers.

Alexander burned the palace complex in 330 BC. Arrian says it was deliberate revenge for Xerxes' burning of Athens; other sources describe a drunken party and a courtesan named Thais suggesting it. Excavation found burnt cedar beams and ash confirming the fire, but cannot say which account is right. The fire baked the tablets and preserved them.

name: Babylon

claims.text: Alexander died at Babylon in June 323 BC.
Babylonian astronomical diaries independently record the death of the king.
The diaries provide a continuous observational record spanning centuries.
The Hanging Gardens were located at Babylon.

summary: The greatest city of Mesopotamia, where Alexander died in 323 BC and where his empire began to fragment.
significance: Its astronomical archives are the longest continuous scientific record from the ancient world, and they date Alexander's death precisely.
body:
Alexander entered Babylon in 331 BC after Gaugamela and was received without a fight. He planned to make it a capital, ordered the ziggurat Etemenanki restored, and died there in June 323 BC.

Babylonian astronomical diaries — nightly records of celestial and civil events kept for some seven centuries — note the death of the king, giving a date that converts to 11 June 323 BC. This is one of very few ancient deaths datable to the day from an independent, contemporary, non-Greek source.

Those same archives contain systematically recorded eclipses, planetary positions and market prices, and they underpin much of modern ancient chronology. The Hanging Gardens, if they existed, have never been located at Babylon; one serious argument places them at Nineveh instead.

name: Tyre

claims.text: Alexander besieged Tyre for seven months in 332 BC and built a causeway to the island.
The causeway permanently joined the island to the mainland.
Tyre was a principal producer of murex purple dye.
The Greek alphabet derives from a Phoenician consonantal script.

summary: The Phoenician island city that resisted Alexander for seven months until he built a causeway to reach it.
significance: Source of the alphabet Greeks adapted, and of the purple dye that made "royal purple" a phrase.
body:
Tyre's main city stood on an island 800 m offshore with walls rising straight from the sea. In 332 BC, refused entry, Alexander built a mole out to it from the mainland — demolishing the old mainland city for stone — under constant attack, then took the walls with ship-mounted siege towers.

The causeway silted up and permanently joined the island to the shore; Tyre is a peninsula today because of a siege.

Tyre produced Tyrian purple from the murex sea snail, requiring thousands of snails per gram, which is why purple signified royalty for two millennia. Phoenician traders spread the consonantal alphabet that Greeks adapted by adding vowels — the ancestor of this text.

name: Issus

claims.text: Alexander defeated Darius III at Issus in 333 BC.
The narrow coastal terrain prevented the Persians from deploying their numbers.
Darius' family was captured after the battle and treated with respect.
The Alexander Mosaic depicts this battle.

summary: The coastal plain where Alexander defeated Darius III in 333 BC and captured the Persian royal family.
significance: The first defeat of a Persian king in person, and the subject of the Alexander Mosaic.
body:
Darius manoeuvred behind Alexander and cut his supply line, forcing a battle on a narrow coastal plain between mountains and sea — ground that neutralised his numerical advantage entirely.

Alexander led the Companion cavalry in an oblique charge across the Pinarus river straight at Darius' position. Darius fled, and his army broke. His mother, wife and children were captured in the camp; Alexander treated them with a courtesy the sources emphasise, and Darius' mother reportedly remained loyal to Alexander afterwards.

The Alexander Mosaic from Pompeii — over a million tesserae, copying a lost Greek painting — shows the moment of the charge, with Darius turning in his chariot to look back.

name: Gaugamela

claims.text: Alexander defeated Darius III at Gaugamela on 1 October 331 BC.
A Babylonian record of a lunar eclipse fixes the date precisely.
Darius prepared the ground in advance for scythed chariots.
The exact battlefield location has been securely identified.

summary: The plain where Alexander destroyed the main Persian army on 1 October 331 BC, on ground Darius had chosen and levelled.
significance: The battle that ended Achaemenid power and delivered the Persian Empire to Alexander.
body:
Darius picked open ground, cleared it for his scythed chariots, and assembled forces from across the empire including elephants. He had every advantage of number and terrain.

Alexander advanced obliquely to the right, drawing the Persian left outward to prevent an outflanking. When a gap opened in the Persian line he drove the Companion cavalry into it in a wedge aimed at Darius, who fled again. On the other flank Parmenion was in serious trouble and Alexander had to break off pursuit to rescue him.

A lunar eclipse eleven days before the battle is recorded in a Babylonian astronomical diary, which fixes the date to 1 October 331 BC — one of the most securely dated events in ancient history.
